messages.author: 7bfe9b28fe0b6ab1
messages.subject: Allometry-corrected shape analysis
parts:
Hello everyone,

I am hoping for some clarification/help on doing allometry-corrected shape analysis. I am analysing the beak shapes of 2 lines of chickens. I have run the following code in Geomorph and get significant P-values suggesting that there is an allometric effect.
             
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(gpa_ppdata, line = pcadata$line) 

#Does shape correlate with size (single multivariate regression)?
fit.size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize), data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.size) 

#Does shape differ between lines (single factor MANOVA)?
fit.line <- procD.lm(coords ~ line, data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.line)

#Does shape differ between lines, while accounting for shape covarying with size (single factor MANCOVA)?
fit.size.line <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * line, data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.size.line)

Now I would like to correct for allometry and use the residuals to generate another PCA plot and run the ANOVAs again but I am just not sure which residuals to use (fit.size, fit.line, or fit.size.line).

For comparing residuals, is the code the same as above? For example,

resid1 <- fit.size$residuals
gdf2 <- geomorph.data.frame(gpa_ppdata, line = pcadata$line, PC1 = pcadata$Comp1, resid1 = resid1)
fit.size.allom <- procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize), data = gdf2, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)

I have read through previous threads about removing the allometric effect but I'm not confident on which code best fits my data. Any help would be very much appreciated!

Thank you,

Sarah

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry-corrected shape analysis
parts:
Sarah,

 

Based on your code, the object fit.size$residuals are in fact the allometry-free residual shape components. However, be aware that if your ancova model fit.size.line displays a significant interaction term with a large effect size (Z-score), this indicates that the allometry patterns differ among groups. In that case, using fit.size$residuals as allometry-free shape is inappropriate, as those residuals are based on a common slope model.

 

And in that case, the residuals from the full model fit.size.line aren’t useful for downstream investigation, as they are not comparable among groups (different allometry lines are fit to each group, so residuals are not from the same thing).

 

Finally, it makes little sense to do the last model you have: procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize).   The residuals already have the effect of log(Csize) removed so this will likely not glean any additional insight.

 

Dean

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry-corrected shape analysis
parts:
Aaron,

 

Yes this topic has been discussed extensively in this blog and elsewhere. A few comments and perspective.

 

First, it is possible that one has a significant linear model effect with no pairwise comparisons being significant. This can occur in univariate anova-type models as well as multivariate models. Usually this boils down to power and sample size: in the aggregate there is enough signal to detect an effect, but broken down by pairs there is insufficient power to identify this (the alternative; a significant pairwise but not full anova is also possible, but for slightly different reasons).

 

Looking at your original model, incorporating the interaction term only provides a modest improvement over the common slopes model: its Z-score (effect size) is 1.87; not hugely impressive. So while there is some evidence of heterogeneity in slopes it is slight.  This then boils down to whether or not you think this represents a real effect or is an artifact. 

 

That’s a hard thing to get at with small sample sizes, but one other option to at least consider is cross-validation. The idea is simple. One fits the full (heterogeneous slopes) model with a subset of data (say 80%) to obtain model parameters. Then, using those parameters one predicts values for the remaining data and calculates the residuals relative to the observed for these. Obtain a variance and repeat, say, 1000 times. Next one does the same procedure for the reduced (common slope) model.  Find the mean of the 1000 error variances for each model. The model with the smaller mean error variance is the better model in terms of cross-validated prediction.

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams (he/him)

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry-corrected shape analysis

 

Hello everyone,

I am using 3D GMM to discern potential intraspecific differences in vertebral shape between life stages of a salamander species. Like Sarah's original post, I am trying to figure out my next step on if I should continue with a common allometric model and correct for allometry or use the unique allometric model and compare slopes. I know the topic of allometric correction has been discussed extensively in this group so forgive me if I missed the post where someone had a similar issue! 

 

I have a significant size:lifestage interaction in the unique allometric model, leading me to believe I should look at the slopes next although there is a small effect size. When I run my pairwise tests nothing comes up significant. So what I'm trying to figure out is does this indicate I can do an allometric correction using the common model, if I set up my analysis wrong in R, or are there different steps I need to take?

 

Thank you in advanced,

 

Aaron

 

 

***Code + Results Below***

 

##Does shape correlate with size

fit.size <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

anova(fit.size)

##Allometry Models

fit.common <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size+lifestage, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

fit.unique <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size*lifestage, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

plotAllometry(fit.unique) is in FIG 1

##Compare Models

anova(fit.common, fit.unique,fit.size, print.progress=FALSE)

Results in FIG 2

##Identify Null Model Design

reveal.model.designs(fit.unique)

Results in FIG 3

fit.null<-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size + lifestage + atlas.size:lifestage, data=sym.gdf,

                   print.progress=FALSE)

##Run a pairwise comparison of slopes

PW<-pairwise(fit.unique, fit.null, groups=lifestage,

             covariate=sym.gdf$atlas.size, print.progress = FALSE)

PW

Different pairwise tests in FIG 4

Looking at your original model, incorporating the interaction term only provides a modest improvement over the common slopes model: its Z-score (effect size) is 1.87; not hugely impressive. So while there is some evidence of heterogeneity in slopes it is slight.  This then boils down to whether or not you think this represents a real effect or is an artifact. 

 

That’s a hard thing to get at with small sample sizes, but one other option to at least consider is cross-validation. The idea is simple. One fits the full (heterogeneous slopes) model with a subset of data (say 80%) to obtain model parameters. Then, using those parameters one predicts values for the remaining data and calculates the residuals relative to the observed for these. Obtain a variance and repeat, say, 1000 times. Next one does the same procedure for the reduced (common slope) model.  Find the mean of the 1000 error variances for each model. The model with the smaller mean error variance is the better model in terms of cross-validated prediction.

 

Dean

Sarah,

 

Based on your code, the object fit.size$residuals are in fact the allometry-free residual shape components. However, be aware that if your ancova model fit.size.line displays a significant interaction term with a large effect size (Z-score), this indicates that the allometry patterns differ among groups. In that case, using fit.size$residuals as allometry-free shape is inappropriate, as those residuals are based on a common slope model.

 

And in that case, the residuals from the full model fit.size.line aren’t useful for downstream investigation, as they are not comparable among groups (different allometry lines are fit to each group, so residuals are not from the same thing).

 

Finally, it makes little sense to do the last model you have: procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize).   The residuals already have the effect of log(Csize) removed so this will likely not glean any additional insight.
